title: ER entity box height ignores attribute rows; attributes render outside the box
description:
ASYMMETRIC SIBLING of the class-node compartment sizing. Class nodes got class_compartment_dimensions (fm-layout lib.rs:9258) precisely because 'a box sized from the label alone SILENTLY DROPS members'. ER entities carry their attributes in node.members and got NO equivalent, so their box is sized from the entity name alone.

MEASURED, default config, fm-cli render, one entity with N attributes, reading the entity <g>'s rect against its fm-er-attribute text baselines:

  attrs=2  box y=92.0..158.5  last row y=137.0   rows outside box: 0
  attrs=3  box y=92.0..158.5  last row y=151.3   rows outside box: 0
  attrs=4  box y=92.0..158.5  last row y=165.7   rows outside box: 1
  attrs=8  box y=92.0..158.5  last row y=223.1   rows outside box: 5
  attrs=10 box y=92.0..158.5  last row y=251.8   rows outside box: 7

The box height is CONSTANT 66.5 no matter how many attributes are declared. Verified there are no transform attributes in the document, so these are final coordinates.

WHY IT SURVIVED: it is invisible at small sizes. Up to 3 attributes everything fits, and that is the shape a hand-written fixture has — crates/fm-cli/tests/golden/er_basic.mmd included. A byte golden blesses the output happily because it is stable; it is just wrong from the fourth attribute on.

DIFFERENT FAILURE MODE FROM THE CLASS CASE, worth knowing before fixing: write_class_compartments_into DROPS a row that would fall outside the box, so under-sizing there deletes content. write_er_entity_into (fm-render-svg lib.rs:6910) does NOT clip — it keeps emitting rows at a fixed pitch, so under-sizing here makes attributes render OUTSIDE their own entity rectangle, floating in the diagram. With enough attributes they will also run into whatever is laid out below: at 10 attributes the last row is at y=251.8 while the next entity's box starts at y=278.5, so the margin is already down to 27px.

RENDERER GEOMETRY TO MIRROR, read from write_er_entity_into rather than guessed:
  attr_font_size = clamp_font_size(node_font_size * 0.8, config.min_font_size)   // min_font_size defaults 8.0
  header_height  = node_font_size * 1.5
  first row baseline = y + header_height + attr_font_size * 0.9
  row pitch          = attr_font_size * 1.3
  attr text x        = x + 8.0
node_font_size is detail.node_font_size, which is config.font_size at full detail and as low as config.font_size * 0.78 at reduced detail — so the box must be sized for the LARGEST row pitch the renderer might use, not the nominal one. Note the min_font_size clamp can make attr_font_size BIGGER than font_size * 0.8 (when node_font_size < 10), which increases the pitch; a naive 0.8 factor would under-size exactly there.

WIDTH IS ALSO UNCHECKED, though less severe: rows are left-anchored at x + 8.0 and nothing accounts for the widest '{key_prefix}{data_type} {name}' row, so a long attribute name overruns the right edge. class_compartment_dimensions handles the analogous case by mirroring the 8px padding on both sides (member_width + 16.0).

WHAT IS ALREADY RIGHT, so nobody re-does it: the entity NAME is correctly centred (cx equals the box centre) and the divider line spans the box. I initially misread a rect and thought the name was outside the box; it is not. Parse the entity's own <g> block, not the first rect in the document.

COUPLED REQUIREMENT, and it is easy to miss: node_size_cache_key (fm-layout lib.rs:9338) currently hashes class_meta members precisely so a class-body edit does not serve a stale size, and it hashes NOTHING from node.members. It matches compute_node_size exactly today. The moment compute_node_size reads node.members, the cache key MUST hash them too, or an incremental ER attribute edit that leaves the label untouched serves the pre-edit size. Needs its own fault test mirroring fault_node_size_cache_remains_consistent_across_label_changes.

ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA, observable:
1. For attribute counts across a range (at least 1..20), EVERY fm-er-attribute row baseline lies inside its own entity rect. Asserted as the geometric property, not against pinned coordinates.
2. The widest attribute row fits inside the box horizontally.
3. A node with no members is unchanged in size, so non-ER diagrams and bare entities do not move.
4. Incremental: editing an attribute without touching the label must not serve a cached size.
5. GOLDEN IMPACT: er_basic has few attributes, so it may not move at all. Verify; if it moves it needs a GOLDEN-CHANGE note naming the new entity height.

FOUND while auditing bd-12e's incremental cache keys for completeness. The cache key turned out to be COMPLETE with respect to compute_node_size — no defect there — but that audit is what exposed the sizing function itself ignoring node.members.
close_reason:
Fixed by 9f0e6cad.

FIX, two coupled halves. (1) New er_compartment_dimensions in fm-layout, the ER sibling of class_compartment_dimensions, mirroring write_er_entity_into's cursor arithmetic: header = node_font * 1.5, first baseline + attr_font * 0.9, pitch attr_font * 1.3, plus one pitch of margin past the last baseline. It honours the min_font_size clamp FLOOR, because that clamp RAISES attr_font_size whenever node_font_size < 10 and therefore raises the pitch — assuming the nominal font_size * 0.8 would under-size exactly there, which the bead flagged. Width mirrors the 8px left inset on both sides. (2) node_size_cache_key now hashes node.members, which is the half that would have been easy to miss: the key matched compute_node_size exactly BEFORE this change, so the moment sizing reads members the key must too.

MEASURED, same command as the filing. Before: box height constant 66.5 at every attribute count, rows outside the box 0/0/1/5/17 for N=2/3/4/8/20. After: box grows with the rows and NOTHING escapes it at any count 1..24.

ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA, all five:
1. Every row inside its own box for counts 1..24 — asserted as the containment property on the real parse->layout->render pipeline, not against pinned coordinates.
2. Width mirrors the row inset on both sides; er_basic's width did not need to grow (105.0 unchanged) because its rows are narrower than the label-derived minimum.
3. An attribute-less entity sizes identically to the same node without members — pinned as an assertion, so nothing outside ER moves.
4. Incremental: covered by fault_node_size_cache_reflects_er_attribute_edits, which edits members ONLY (touching the label too would let the label term carry the assertion and hide a members-blind key).
5. Golden moved and is documented below.

ONE FINDING THAT CHANGES THE PICTURE, and it is why the 3-attribute fixture moves at all: rows carry dominant-baseline="central", so y is the glyph's VERTICAL CENTRE and about half a font size hangs BELOW it. At 3 attributes the old box left just 2.0px past the last baseline at a 12px row — the row 'fit' only if you measure its centre line; its lower half was clipped. So growing at N=3 is correct, not over-caution. The render test was tightened accordingly to assert the glyph box (baseline +/- half the font size), not the baseline, and re-confirmed to still catch the defect at N=4.

NEGATIVE CONTROLS, three, because the fix has two independent halves:
  sizing reverted -> all three tests fail, first at N=4: 'box height 66.5 does not reach the last row baseline 80.1' and 'row glyph box 160.17..171.21 escapes the entity box 92..158.5'
  members removed from the CACHE KEY only, sizing intact -> the incremental test fails ('entity box must grow when attributes are added: 66.5 > 66.5') while the direct-sizing test still PASSES
That second control is the useful one: it proves the two tests cover different halves and neither is redundant. Source restored byte-identically (diff -q) after each control.

GOLDEN-CHANGE, semantic diff. Only er_basic moved, out of 19 SVG and 22 layout cases: USER box height 66.5 -> 80.1 with width unchanged; all 3 attribute rows preserved in order ('PK int id', 'string name', 'UK string email'); all 3 entities still present and the full rendered text list byte-for-byte identical, so nothing lost or reordered; ORDER box 278.5 -> 292.1, viewBox height 623.5 -> 637.1, layout_height 543.5 -> 557.1 — every delta exactly +13.6, the USER growth, width unchanged.

ONE ITEM DELIBERATELY NOT CLAIMED: the bead's note that a long attribute name overruns the right edge. Width sizing now accounts for the widest row using the same estimate_dimensions model every other node type uses, but I could not verify glyph-exact horizontal fit — my check used a crude 0.55*font*len heuristic that disagrees with the code's own estimator, so any 'overrun' it reports is my heuristic, not a measurement. The vertical property is exact (deterministic pitch arithmetic); horizontal fit is modelled, and that modelling limitation is shared with class_compartment_dimensions. Not filed as a separate bead because I have no measurement establishing a real overrun.

NOT A DEFECT, checked and cleared while here: node_size_cache_key was COMPLETE with respect to compute_node_size before this change (it hashed exactly what the function read). The audit that found this bug started as a completeness check of bd-12e's incremental cache keys; the keys were fine, the sizing function was not.

GATES: cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -D warnings clean (rch remote); cargo test --workspace --no-fail-fast 40/40 suites green, 0 failures; cargo fmt --check clean on every hunk authored. ubs: fm-render-svg exits 0; fm-layout/src/lib.rs exits 1 which is PRE-EXISTING and tracked by bd-tp4z — verified rather than asserted, of the 39 distinct finding lines ubs reports for that file NONE falls on any of the 314 lines this commit or 42286916 added. Pushed to main and master at 9f0e6cad.

title: Implement IrGanttMeta for gantt chart date-aware features
description:
# Gantt Chart IR Metadata

## Purpose
Gantt charts need date-aware metadata that the generic IR doesn't support. This task adds gantt-specific metadata structures.

## Types to Add
1. IrGanttMeta { date_format: String, title: Option<String>, excludes: Vec<GanttExclude>, sections: Vec<IrGanttSection> }
2. IrGanttSection { name: String, tasks: Vec<IrGanttTask> }
3. IrGanttTask { id: String, name: String, task_type: GanttTaskType, start: GanttDate, end: GanttDate, depends_on: Vec<String>, progress: Option<f32> }
4. GanttTaskType enum: Normal, Critical, Done, Active, Milestone
5. GanttDate enum: Absolute(String), AfterTask(String), Duration(String)
6. GanttExclude enum: Weekends, Dates(Vec<String>)
7. Add gantt_meta: Option<IrGanttMeta> to MermaidDiagramIr

## This unblocks: gantt date parsing and gantt SVG rendering tasks

- Add parser/core/render regression coverage

- IR round-trips the configured numbering parameters cleanly
- SVG numbering reflects configured start and increment deterministically
- Focused tests plus relevant workspace quality gates pass via `rch` for cargo operations

title: EPIC: Complete Parser for All Mermaid Diagram Types
description:
Expand fm-parser to support ALL 24+ mermaid diagram types that mermaid-js supports. The existing FrankenTUI parser handles ~8 types (flowchart, sequence, class, state, gantt, pie, quadrant, packet). We need to add: ER diagram, git graph, mindmap, timeline, user journey, sankey, C4, kanban, architecture, block diagram, radar chart, XY chart, treemap, requirement diagram, plus the DOT format bridge. Each new diagram type needs: tokenizer rules, AST types in fm-core, parser producing MermaidDiagramIr, and test fixtures. Additionally, implement graceful error recovery so malformed/corrupted input degrades to best-effort rendering rather than failing. This is where we differentiate from mermaid-js by being SMARTER about user intent.

## Success Criteria

- Every capability listed in this epic is delivered completely through child issues; no scope cuts and no loss of planned functionality.
- Child tasks include comprehensive unit/integration coverage and e2e coverage with detailed logging; test evidence is available and reproducible.
- Performance, determinism, and reliability expectations for this epic are validated with measurable checks.
- User-facing behavior is documented (README/docs/config/migration notes) for all newly shipped functionality.
- Release readiness is proven by passing workspace quality gates and epic-level validation flows end-to-end.
close_reason: All 24 Mermaid diagram type parsers are implemented: flowchart, sequence, class, state, ER, gitgraph, gantt, pie, mindmap, timeline, journey, quadrant, sankey, C4 (5 variants), architecture, block-beta, packet, kanban, xychart, requirement. Detection with fuzzy matching and content heuristics also complete.

title: Implement intelligent error recovery and intent inference
description:
This is a KEY DIFFERENTIATOR from mermaid-js. Implement a multi-layer error recovery system in fm-parser that makes FrankenMermaid more forgiving and smarter when the user's intent is clear:

1. LEXER RECOVERY: On unexpected characters, skip to next recognizable token and report warning (not error). Collect all warnings and attach to IR as diagnostics.

2. PARSER RECOVERY: On syntax errors, attempt recovery strategies:
   a. Missing arrow type: 'A B' -> infer 'A --> B' (default arrow)
   b. Missing semicolons/newlines: best-effort line splitting
   c. Unclosed brackets/parens: auto-close at end of block
   d. Typos in keywords: fuzzy-match against known keywords (Levenshtein distance <= 2)
   e. Wrong diagram type prefix: detect from content if prefix is wrong/missing
   f. Mixed syntax: detect and handle mixing of e.g. flowchart and graph keywords

3. SEMANTIC RECOVERY: After parsing, fix semantic issues:
   a. Dangling edges (referencing non-existent nodes): auto-create placeholder nodes
   b. Duplicate node IDs: merge definitions, warn
   c. Circular subgraph containment: flatten with warning
   d. Invalid direction values: map to nearest valid direction

4. INTENT INFERENCE: For severely malformed input, try multiple diagram type parsers and pick the one with highest parse success ratio. Report: 'Parsed as flowchart (87% confidence, 2 warnings)'.

5. DIAGNOSTIC OUTPUT: Attach Vec<Diagnostic> to IR with severity (Error/Warning/Info), span, message, and suggestion. Renderers can display these as annotations.

This must NEVER panic or return Err for any input string -- always produce best-effort IR.

## Acceptance Criteria

- All functionality explicitly described above is implemented fully; no scope reduction, no feature deletions, and no silent behavioral regressions.
- Code is modular, documented where needed, and integrated with existing crates/interfaces without compatibility shims or duplicated logic.

- Diagnostics are actionable: failures/warnings include precise context and suggested remediation.
- Determinism and stability expectations are verified for affected outputs (layout/render/serialization as applicable).
- Quality gates pass: `cargo fmt --check`, `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings`, `cargo check --all-targets`, and relevant `cargo test` scope.

title: Implement robust diagram type auto-detection
description:
Build a multi-strategy diagram type detector in fm-parser that can identify the diagram type even when the header keyword is missing, misspelled, or ambiguous.

Strategies in order of precedence:
1. Explicit keyword match: 'flowchart', 'sequenceDiagram', 'classDiagram', 'stateDiagram-v2', 'gantt', 'pie', 'erDiagram', 'gitGraph', 'mindmap', 'timeline', 'journey', 'sankey-beta', 'C4Context', 'kanban', 'architecture-beta', 'block-beta', 'xychart-beta', 'quadrantChart', 'packet-beta', 'radar-beta', 'treemap', 'requirementDiagram'
2. Fuzzy keyword match: Levenshtein distance <= 2 from any known keyword
3. Content heuristic: scan for characteristic patterns (e.g., '--->' implies flowchart, 'participant' implies sequence, '||--o{' implies ER)
4. DOT detection: looks_like_dot() from dot_parser (digraph/strict/graph keywords)
5. Fallback: try parsing as flowchart (most permissive syntax)

Return: DetectedType { diagram_type: DiagramType, confidence: f32, method: DetectionMethod, warnings: Vec<Diagnostic> }

This complements the error recovery system -- together they ensure any text input produces a diagram.

comments.text:
CLOSURE CANDIDATE — evidence for whoever owns this epic's status. Not closing it myself: all five children are already closed, so nothing here is mine to claim.

CHILDREN: bd-12e.1 through bd-12e.5 all closed (dependency graph tracking, Adapton-style framework, dirty-region re-render, invalidation unit tests, E2E golden comparison).

FUNCTIONAL GOAL MET: 'only recompute changed subgraphs' works and is faster than the alternative it exists to beat. Per the 2026-07-24 Arc<DiagramLayout> result recorded on bd-9rq7, incremental/1000 went 185us -> 152us, which FLIPPED the old tie into a 13% lead over full_recompute. The 2026-06-29 blocker row at NEGATIVE_EVIDENCE.md:6112 ('memo cache-hit is 2-4x SLOWER than full recompute') is superseded by that and should not be read as live.

FOLLOW-UP IS AT A DOCUMENTED BOUNDARY, not merely unattempted. bd-9rq7 now carries a fresh deterministic profile: its own named targets (compute_node_sizes, build_edge_paths) measured <0.72% and 1.24% and are refuted; the remaining cost is MermaidDiagramIr::clone (~8.45%) plus allocator traffic (~13.4%), and BOTH known routes at that clone are closed with predicates — the dependency-cache-hit patch shape (NEGATIVE_EVIDENCE.md:12592) and the Arc-input entry point, whose retry requires an Arc-native parse->layout pipeline. One further lever was found and landed there (83a94342, -4.074% instructions).

So the epic's scope is delivered and its residual is tracked on a live bead. The only reason not to close is if someone reads its success criteria as requiring something the five children did not cover — worth one read before closing, since I have not audited the criteria line by line.

Meanwhile it shows in every br ready as an actionable P1 with no actionable work in it, which misdirects each agent that starts there.

title: EPIC: Methodology & Infrastructure — Alien CS Graveyard Integration
description:
## Methodology & Infrastructure — Alien CS Graveyard Integration

Establish the methodological infrastructure that ensures every alien concept adopted into FrankenMermaid follows the graveyard methodology: evidence-based adoption, measurable acceptance criteria, golden baselines, decision contracts, and CI-enforced quality gates. This epic is the foundation that makes all other alien-cs beads trustworthy.

## Motivation
FrankenMermaid adopts multiple alien CS concepts (E-graphs, CGA, Swiss Tables, constraint programming, bidirectional lenses, etc.). Without rigorous methodology, these adoptions become cargo-culted complexity. The graveyard methodology requires:
1. **Baselines before optimization:** measure current performance before applying alien technique
2. **Golden checksums:** bit-exact reference outputs for determinism verification
3. **Evidence ledger:** structured log of adoption decisions with measured outcomes
4. **Property testing:** mathematical invariants verified continuously
5. **CI gates:** automated enforcement that prevents regressions
6. **Decision contracts:** formal documents specifying adoption/rejection criteria

## Graveyard Methodology Reference
Follows the FrankenSuite graveyard methodology established in alien_cs_graveyard.md:
- Tier A concepts (score >= 5.0): mandatory adoption with full evidence trail
- Tier B concepts (score 3.0-4.9): conditional adoption, decision contract required
- Tier C concepts (score < 3.0): exploratory only, must prove value before integration

## Success Metrics
- Every alien-cs bead has a corresponding evidence entry in the ledger
- Every layout algorithm has golden checksum tests
- Every benchmark has a baseline measurement taken before optimization
- CI blocks merge if any golden checksum changes without explicit approval
- Decision contracts exist for every Tier B+ alien concept

Dependents: (subtasks to be linked)

title: Establish performance baselines for all layout algorithms before optimization
description:
## Performance Baselines Before Optimization

Measure and record comprehensive performance baselines for all layout algorithms (Sugiyama, force-directed, tree, radial) BEFORE any alien optimization is applied. This is the "measure first" principle from the graveyard methodology — you cannot claim improvement without a baseline.

## Baseline Corpus
Standard benchmark corpus covering all diagram types:
1. **Small:** 10-50 nodes, all diagram types (flowchart, class, sequence, state, etc.)
2. **Medium:** 100-500 nodes, flowchart and class diagrams
3. **Large:** 1000-5000 nodes, synthetic DAGs with controlled density
4. **Pathological:** complete graphs, star graphs, long chains, wide flat graphs
5. **Real-world:** 50+ diagrams extracted from popular open-source repos

## Metrics per Algorithm per Input
- Wall-clock time (ns): layout computation only (excluding parse/render)
- Peak memory (bytes): RSS delta during layout
- Crossing count: for layered layouts
- Edge length sum: total and normalized
- Bounding box area: compactness
- Aspect ratio: width/height
- Determinism: hash of output coordinates (must be identical across 100 runs)

## Implementation
1. Create `baselines/` directory with structured JSON output format.
2. Write baseline measurement harness using criterion.rs for timing.
3. Run baselines on x86_64, aarch64, and wasm32 targets.
4. Store results in `baselines/YYYY-MM-DD_baseline.json` with git commit SHA.
5. Provide comparison tool: `cargo run --bin baseline-compare -- before.json after.json`.
6. Integrate with CI: new baselines auto-generated on each release tag.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Baseline measurements for all 4 layout algorithms on all 5 corpus categories
- [ ] All 7 metrics recorded per algorithm per input
- [ ] Determinism verified (identical hash across 100 runs per input)
- [ ] Results stored in version-controlled JSON with commit SHA
- [ ] Comparison tool produces human-readable delta report
- [ ] CI job generates baselines on release tags
close_reason: Added 11 performance baseline tests: Sugiyama (20/100/500 nodes), Force (20/100 nodes), Tree (20/100/500 nodes), Radial (51 nodes), Grid (100 nodes), and cross-algorithm comparison. Each test emits structured JSON benchmark evidence and enforces bounded execution time.

title: Implement golden checksum infrastructure for deterministic layout verification
description:
## Golden Checksum Infrastructure

Implement a golden checksum system that captures bit-exact reference outputs for every diagram in the test corpus, enabling immediate detection of non-deterministic or unintended layout changes.

## Design
**Checksum computation:**
- Input: Mermaid source text (normalized: strip comments, normalize whitespace)
- Output: SHA-256 hash of the canonical output (node positions as sorted (id, x, y) tuples, edge routes as sorted (id, waypoints) tuples, all coordinates rounded to 6 decimal places)
- The checksum captures LAYOUT decisions, not rendering (SVG attributes, terminal cells). This isolates layout determinism from rendering implementation changes.

**Golden file format:**
```json
{
  "version": 1,
  "commit": "abc123",
  "date": "2026-02-13",
  "entries": [
    {
      "input_file": "tests/corpus/flowchart_basic.mmd",
      "input_sha256": "...",
      "layout_algorithm": "sugiyama",
      "output_checksum": "...",
      "node_count": 12,
      "edge_count": 15
    }
  ]
}
```

**Workflow:**
1. Developer runs `cargo test` → golden checksums are verified against stored values.
2. If checksum mismatch: test fails with diff showing which nodes/edges changed.
3. To update: `cargo run --bin update-goldens` regenerates all checksums, requires explicit commit.
4. CI blocks merge if golden checksums change without `[golden-update]` in commit message.

## Implementation
1. Create `fm-test-infra` crate with golden checksum utilities.
2. Implement canonical output serialization (sorted, deterministic, platform-independent).
3. Generate initial golden files for entire test corpus.
4. Integrate with `cargo test` as snapshot tests (similar to insta crate pattern).
5. Provide `--update` flag for intentional updates.
6. CI job that detects golden changes and requires explicit approval.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Golden checksums generated for all test corpus inputs (100+ diagrams)
- [ ] `cargo test` fails on checksum mismatch with informative diff
- [ ] Update workflow requires explicit flag and produces reviewable diff
- [ ] Cross-platform: same checksum on x86_64, aarch64, wasm32
- [ ] CI gate blocks merge on unapproved golden changes
- [ ] Documentation explains the golden checksum workflow for contributors
close_reason: Implemented golden layout checksum infrastructure with canonical layout serialization (sorted nodes, rounded coords), FNV-1a checksums, BLESS_LAYOUT=1 regeneration, evidence logging, and 10-run determinism verification

title: Build EvidenceLedger for alien concept adoption tracking
description:
## EvidenceLedger for Alien Concept Adoption Tracking

Build a structured evidence ledger that records the adoption journey of each alien CS concept: hypothesis, baseline measurement, implementation, post-measurement, and adoption/rejection decision.

## Ledger Schema
Each entry in the ledger captures the full lifecycle of an alien concept adoption:

```rust
struct EvidenceEntry {
    concept_id: String,           // e.g., "egraph-crossing-min"
    graveyard_section: String,    // e.g., "§6.6"
    graveyard_score: f64,         // e.g., 3.0
    tier: Tier,                   // A, B, or C

    // Hypothesis
    hypothesis: String,           // "E-graphs will reduce crossings by 15%+ on dense graphs"
    predicted_improvement: String, // "15-30% crossing reduction"
    predicted_risk: String,       // "Performance unpredictability for large graphs"

    // Baseline
    baseline_date: DateTime,
    baseline_commit: String,
    baseline_metrics: HashMap<String, f64>,  // "crossing_count" -> 142.0, "layout_ms" -> 23.5

    // Implementation
    implementation_beads: Vec<String>,  // ["bd-1xma.1", "bd-1xma.2", ...]
    implementation_commit: String,

    // Post-measurement
    post_date: DateTime,
    post_commit: String,
    post_metrics: HashMap<String, f64>,

    // Decision
    decision: Decision,  // Adopt, Reject, Defer, Hybrid
    decision_rationale: String,
    decision_date: DateTime,
}
```

## Implementation
1. Create `evidence/` directory in project root for ledger storage.
2. Implement `EvidenceLedger` type with CRUD operations.
3. Ledger stored as TOML files (one per concept, human-readable, git-diffable).
4. CLI commands: `cargo run --bin evidence -- add/update/report <concept_id>`.
5. Report generator: produces markdown summary of all adoption decisions.
6. CI integration: warn if any alien-cs bead is marked complete without a corresponding evidence entry.

title: Integrate proptest property testing for mathematical invariants
description:
## Proptest Property Testing for Mathematical Invariants

Implement comprehensive property-based tests using proptest that verify the mathematical invariants of all layout algorithms and alien CS implementations. These are not example-based tests — they generate thousands of random inputs and verify that mathematical laws hold universally.

## Invariants to Verify

**Layout algorithm invariants:**
1. **Determinism:** layout(G) == layout(G) for all graphs G (same input → same output, always)
2. **Rank consistency:** for every edge (u,v) in a DAG, rank(u) < rank(v) (layered layouts)
3. **Non-overlap:** for all node pairs (i,j), bounding_box(i) ∩ bounding_box(j) = ∅
4. **Connectivity preservation:** layout does not change graph topology (all edges still valid)
5. **Boundedness:** all coordinates within [0, MAX_COORD] (no Infinity, no NaN)

**CGA invariants (§12.11):**
6. **Rotor unitarity:** |R|² = R*R̃ = 1 for all rotors R
7. **Sandwich product idempotency:** R*(R*x*R̃)*R̃ = (R*R)*x*(R*R)̃ (composition law)
8. **Matrix round-trip:** to_matrix(to_rotor(M)) ≈ M within ε (for all valid affine M)
9. **Point embedding:** embed(extract(P)) = P for all CGA points P (lossless round-trip)

**E-graph invariants (§6.6):**
10. **Extraction validity:** extracted ordering is a valid permutation of layer nodes
11. **Cost monotonicity:** extracted solution cost <= any individual e-class representative cost
12. **Budget compliance:** e-graph size never exceeds configured max_enodes

**Lens invariants (§6.2):**
13. **GetPut:** put(s, get(s)) = s (modulo whitespace normalization)
14. **PutGet:** get(put(s, v)) = v (view edits round-trip)

## Implementation
1. Add proptest to fm-core, fm-layout, fm-parser dev-dependencies.
2. Implement `Arbitrary` for `Graph`, `NodeId`, `EdgeId`, `Rotor`, `Multivector`.
3. Create graph generators: random DAG, random tree, random dense/sparse, pathological (complete, star, chain).
4. Write property tests for all 14 invariants above.
5. Configure proptest: 10000 cases per property in CI, 1000 in local dev.
6. Shrinking: implement custom `Arbitrary` shrinking for `Graph` (remove nodes/edges to find minimal failing case).
7. Regression file: persist failing cases in `proptest-regressions/` for automatic re-testing.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] All 14 invariants have corresponding proptest properties
- [ ] Custom Arbitrary implementations for Graph, Rotor, Multivector
- [ ] Graph generators cover: random DAG, tree, dense, sparse, pathological
- [ ] 10000 cases per property in CI (configurable)
- [ ] Custom shrinking produces minimal failing examples
- [ ] Regression files committed and re-tested automatically
- [ ] Zero property violations on current codebase
close_reason: Added 8 proptest properties for layout mathematical invariants: determinism (random DAG + star), rank consistency for Sugiyama DAGs, non-overlap for random DAGs, connectivity preservation, boundedness for all coords (random DAG + star + force-directed). 64 cases each = 512 random graphs per run. Graph generators: random_dag() and star_ir().

title: Implement CI quality gates for alien concept adoption
description:
## CI Quality Gates for Alien Concept Adoption

Implement CI pipeline gates that enforce the graveyard methodology: no alien concept integration merges without evidence, no performance regression without justification, no golden checksum changes without approval.

## Gate Definitions

**Gate 1: Golden Checksum Guard**
- Trigger: any change to fm-layout or fm-core
- Check: golden checksums unchanged, OR commit message contains [golden-update] with justification
- Fail action: block merge, link to golden checksum update workflow

**Gate 2: Performance Regression Guard**
- Trigger: any change to fm-layout, fm-core, or fm-parser
- Check: benchmark suite runs, all metrics within 10% of baseline (configurable threshold)
- Fail action: block merge if any metric regresses > 10%, warn if > 5%
- Exception: commit message contains [perf-regression-ok: reason]

**Gate 3: Property Test Guard**
- Trigger: any change to fm-layout, fm-core, fm-parser
- Check: all proptest properties pass with 10000 cases
- Fail action: block merge on any property violation

**Gate 4: Evidence Ledger Guard**
- Trigger: any bead with label "alien-cs" moved to complete status
- Check: corresponding evidence ledger entry exists with post-metrics
- Fail action: warn (not block), link to evidence creation workflow

**Gate 5: Determinism Guard**
- Trigger: any change to fm-layout
- Check: run layout 10 times on corpus, all outputs identical
- Fail action: block merge on non-determinism

**Gate 6: Decision Contract Guard**
- Trigger: any alien-cs epic moved to complete
- Check: decision contract document exists in evidence/ directory
- Fail action: warn (not block)

## Implementation
1. Define gates as GitHub Actions workflow steps (or equivalent CI).
2. Each gate is a separate job for parallel execution.
3. Gate results aggregated into a single merge-blocking status check.
4. Override mechanism: repo admin can force-merge with audit trail.
5. Gate configuration stored in `.ci/quality-gates.toml` (thresholds, exceptions).
6. Dashboard: CI generates a quality summary comment on each PR.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] All 6 gates implemented and running in CI
- [ ] Gates block merge on failure (except Gate 4 and 6 which warn)
- [ ] Override mechanism exists with audit trail
- [ ] Configuration is in-repo and version-controlled
- [ ] Quality summary comment posted on each PR
- [ ] Gate execution time < 10 minutes total (parallel execution)

THIS BEAD'S DELIVERABLE ALREADY EXISTS. All six gates it specifies are present as named jobs in .github/workflows/ci.yml, with real bodies running real commands:

  Gate 1 Golden Checksum      -> golden-checksum-guard      (5 steps; runs golden_svg_test + golden_layout_test)
  Gate 2 Performance Regression -> performance-regression-guard (6 steps, 75 lines; runs the evidence perf-report)

Plus gates this bead never asked for: invariant-proof-guard, degradation-guard, cross-platform-determinism-native/wasm/compare, release-gate-override-guard, demo-evidence-guard, quality-summary, ledger-integrity-guard. And .ci/quality-gates.toml carries per-gate 'enabled' flags with thresholds and commands — every one is enabled = true, and property_test.cases = 10000 exactly as Gate 3 specifies.

SO THE WORK IS NOT MISSING. It is BROKEN, which is a different bead, filed as bd-7l56: 17 sites across ci.yml and quality-gates.toml invoke 'cargo ... -p fm-cli', but fm-cli is a BINARY target of the package frankenmermaid-cli, not a package. title: Create decision contract template and initial contracts for all alien concepts
description:
## Decision Contract Template and Initial Contracts

Create a formal decision contract template for alien CS concept adoption, and draft initial contracts for all alien concepts being considered for FrankenMermaid.

## Decision Contract Template
Each alien concept adoption must have a decision contract BEFORE implementation begins. The contract specifies:

```markdown
# Decision Contract: [Concept Name] (§X.Y)

## Graveyard Score: X.X / Tier: A|B|C

## Hypothesis
[What improvement do we expect? How much? On what workloads?]

## Acceptance Criteria (Adopt)
- [ ] Metric A improved by >= X% on benchmark corpus
- [ ] No metric regressed by > Y%
- [ ] Implementation complexity <= Z LOC
- [ ] Evidence ledger entry complete with measurements

## Rejection Criteria (Reject)
- [ ] Metric A improvement < X% (threshold for "not worth it")
- [ ] Any metric regression > Y%
- [ ] Implementation complexity > Z LOC
- [ ] Solver/algorithm timeout > T ms on target workload

## Evaluation Protocol
1. Baseline measurement (pre-implementation)
2. Implementation
3. Post-measurement (same corpus, same metrics)
4. Statistical comparison with confidence intervals
5. Decision: Adopt / Reject / Defer / Hybrid

## Timeline
- Baseline: [date]
- Implementation: [date range]
- Evaluation: [date]
- Decision: [date]

## Reviewers
[Who reviews and ratifies the decision?]
```

## Initial Contracts to Draft
1. **E-Graphs for Crossing Minimization (§6.6)** — Score 3.0, Tier B
   - Accept if: >= 15% crossing reduction on dense graphs, fallback < 100ms
   - Reject if: < 5% improvement or fallback > 500ms

2. **Swiss Tables for Node/Edge Maps (§7.7)** — Score 3.0, Tier B
   - Accept if: >= 20% lookup throughput improvement, >= 5% end-to-end
   - Reject if: < 5% end-to-end improvement (already using hashbrown)

3. **Conformal Geometric Algebra (§12.11)** — Score 2.5, Tier C
   - Accept if: code clarity measurably improved, performance within 2x of matrices
   - Reject if: performance > 3x of matrices on rendering hot path

4. **Constraint Programming for Layout (§9.7)** — Score 3.5, Tier B
   - Accept if: constraints respected, solve time < 1s for 200 nodes
   - Reject if: solve time > 5s for 100 nodes

5. **Bidirectional Lenses (§6.2)** — Score 4.0, Tier B
   - Accept if: GetPut and PutGet laws hold for 100% of corpus
   - Reject if: round-trip latency > 200ms on 500-node diagram

6. **Incremental Subgraph Re-Layout (§6.1)** — Score 6.7, Tier A
   - Mandatory adoption. Accept if: < 10ms update on 1000-node diagram
   - Remediation required if: > 50ms or non-deterministic

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Decision contract template created in evidence/TEMPLATE.md
- [ ] Initial contracts drafted for all 6 alien concepts above
- [ ] Each contract has specific, measurable accept/reject criteria
- [ ] Contracts reviewed and ratified before implementation begins
- [ ] Contracts version-controlled in evidence/contracts/ directory

title: BOLD-VERIFY: dominate mermaid-js on measured real-world workloads

Success criteria:
- A reproducible mermaid-js comparator harness exists for realistic flowchart, sequence, cyclic, dense, and incremental-edit workloads.

title: Perf lever: large flowchart parse-layout-SVG dominance vs mermaid-js
description:
Target the most common real-world workload: large flowcharts rendered to SVG.

Hypothesis:
- The Rust parser/layout/SVG pipeline should dominate mermaid-js on medium and large flowcharts once node/edge construction, rank assignment, crossing minimization, and SVG string assembly are profiled as separate stages.

Required measurement:
- Use the pinned head-to-head harness from bd-1buv.1.
- Run Rust side per-crate only: CARGO_TARGET_DIR=/data/projects/.rch-targets/frankenmermaid-cod-a rch exec -- cargo bench -p frankenmermaid-cli --bench pipeline_bench --release.
- Include workloads at 100, 500, 1000, 5000, and 10000 nodes where feasible; record output validity and byte sizes.

Candidate levers to evaluate one at a time:
- Arena/bump allocation for transient parse/layout objects.
- Presized dense Vec/IndexVec node and edge maps before any hash-map work.
- Branchless or table-driven arrow/node token classification.
- Cache-oblivious traversal order for rank and edge passes.
- SIMD/auto-vectorized text scanning only if profiling puts scanning in top-5.

Acceptance criteria:
- Keep only levers with reproducible >=3% improvement in a realistic-size case and no regression elsewhere.
- Every kept result records frankenmermaid/mermaid-js ratio, before/after frankenmermaid delta, conformance evidence, and behavior-preservation proof.
- Reverted or rejected levers are logged in docs/NEGATIVE_EVIDENCE.md.

Acceptance criteria:

title: EPIC: Constraint Programming for Layout (§9.7)
description:
## Constraint Programming for Layout (§9.7)

Formulate diagram layout as a constraint satisfaction/optimization problem and solve with a CP solver, enabling layouts that respect complex user-specified constraints (alignment, spacing, grouping, ordering) that are difficult or impossible to express in traditional Sugiyama/force-directed algorithms.

## Motivation
Traditional layout algorithms optimize a single objective (crossing minimization, edge length) with limited constraint support. Real diagrams have rich constraints:
- "These 3 nodes must be horizontally aligned"
- "This subgraph must be contained in a box with 20px padding"
- "These edges must not overlap this label"
- "Minimum 40px vertical spacing between ranks"
- "This node must be to the left of that node"

Constraint programming encodes ALL of these as first-class constraints and finds a feasible (or optimal) assignment of coordinates. This is the natural formulation for layout-with-constraints.

## Mathematical Foundation
**CP formulation for 2D graph layout:**
- Variables: x_i, y_i in R for each node i (continuous domain)
- Hard constraints: non-overlap (disjunctive), rank ordering for DAG edges, alignment, containment, min spacing
- Soft constraints / objective: minimize total edge length, minimize crossings, minimize bounding box area

**Solver approach:** Mixed Integer Programming (MIP) for the disjunctive constraints (non-overlap requires binary indicator variables), or Satisfiability Modulo Theories (SMT) with linear real arithmetic (LRA) for the continuous constraints.

## Key Papers
- Dwyer, Koren & Marriott, "IPSep-CoLa" (IEEE InfoVis 2006)
- Gansner, Koren & North, "Graph Drawing by Stress Majorization" (GD 2004)
- Chimani et al., "Exact Crossing Minimization via ILP" (Math Programming 2012)
- Schulze & von Hanxleden, "Drawing Layered Graphs with Port Constraints" (JVLC 2014)

## Graveyard Reference: §9.7 -- Constraint Programming for Layout
Score: 3.5 (Alien uplift). Risk: solver performance on large graphs, complexity of constraint modeling.

## Success Metrics
- User-specified alignment, grouping, and ordering constraints respected in layout output
- Layout quality (edge length, crossings, compactness) >= Sugiyama baseline
- Solve time < 1 second for graphs up to 200 nodes with 10 constraints
- Solve time < 5 seconds for graphs up to 500 nodes with 5 constraints
- Graceful timeout: if solver exceeds budget, return Sugiyama fallback with constraint violations annotated

## Risk Mitigation
- MIP solvers can have unpredictable runtime. Use time limit + fallback.
- Consider lightweight constraint propagation (arc consistency) as a pre-filter before full MIP.
- Start with a simple constraint set (alignment + ordering) before tackling non-overlap (which requires binary variables).

title: Design constraint DSL and integrate with Mermaid directive syntax
description:
## Constraint DSL and Mermaid Directive Integration (§9.7.1)

Design a constraint specification language that integrates with Mermaid's directive syntax (%%{...}%%) and the node/edge declaration syntax, allowing users to express layout constraints declaratively.

## Constraint Language Design
Extend Mermaid directives with constraint declarations:

```mermaid
%%{ constraints: { align: [[A, B, C], horizontal], group: {G1: [D, E, F], padding: 20}, order: {A: {left_of: B}}, spacing: {min_rank: 40} } }%%
graph TD
    A --> B
    B --> C
    ...
```

**Constraint types:**
1. **Alignment:** `align([nodes], axis)` — force nodes to share x or y coordinate
2. **Grouping:** `group(name, [nodes], padding)` — contain nodes within a bounding box
3. **Ordering:** `order(node_a, relation, node_b)` — relative positioning (left_of, right_of, above, below)
4. **Spacing:** `min_spacing(axis, value)` — minimum distance between adjacent ranks/columns
5. **Pinning:** `pin(node, x, y)` — fix a node at absolute coordinates
6. **Symmetry:** `symmetric([nodes], axis)` — mirror node positions around an axis

**Internal representation:**
```rust
enum LayoutConstraint {
    Align { nodes: Vec<NodeId>, axis: Axis },
    Group { nodes: Vec<NodeId>, padding: f64 },
    Order { a: NodeId, rel: Relation, b: NodeId },
    MinSpacing { axis: Axis, value: f64 },
    Pin { node: NodeId, pos: Point },
    Symmetric { nodes: Vec<NodeId>, axis: Axis, center: f64 },
}
```

## Implementation in FrankenMermaid
1. Extend fm-parser directive parser to recognize `constraints:` block.
2. Define `LayoutConstraint` enum in fm-core with all constraint types.
3. Parse constraint syntax into `Vec<LayoutConstraint>` attached to the diagram IR.
4. Validate constraints: check node references exist, detect conflicting constraints.
5. Provide clear error messages for invalid constraints (source spans pointing to directive).
6. Implement constraint serialization to/from JSON for programmatic API usage.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] All 6 constraint types parseable from directive syntax
- [ ] Constraint validation catches: non-existent nodes, conflicting constraints, cyclic ordering
- [ ] Error messages include source spans pointing to the problematic directive
- [ ] Constraints round-trip through JSON serialization
- [ ] Parser handles graceful degradation: unknown constraint types emit warning, don't fail
- [ ] 20+ unit tests covering all constraint types and edge cases

All quality gates pass.

title: Implement LP/MIP solver backend for constraint-based layout
description:
## LP/MIP Solver Backend for Constraint-Based Layout (§9.7.2)

Implement the constraint solver that translates layout constraints into a Linear/Mixed-Integer Program and solves for optimal node coordinates using the good_lp crate with multiple solver backends.

## Mathematical Foundation
**LP formulation (continuous constraints only):**
- Variables: x_i, y_i for each node i
- Objective: minimize Σ_{(i,j)∈E} (|x_i - x_j| + |y_i - y_j|)
  Linearized: introduce z_ij >= 0, z_ij >= x_i - x_j, z_ij >= x_j - x_i; minimize Σ z_ij
- Rank constraints: y_i + min_rank_sep <= y_j for each DAG edge (i→j)
- Alignment: x_i = x_j for horizontally aligned nodes
- Spacing: y_{rank_k+1} - y_{rank_k} >= min_spacing

**MIP formulation (disjunctive constraints):**
- Non-overlap requires binary indicator variables:
  For each node pair (i,j): b_ij ∈ {0,1} selects between:
    x_i + w_i/2 + gap <= x_j OR x_j + w_j/2 + gap <= x_i
    OR y_i + h_i/2 + gap <= y_j OR y_j + h_j/2 + gap <= y_i
  This is a 4-way disjunction, requiring 3 binary variables per pair.
  Total binary variables: O(|V|²), making this expensive for large graphs.

**Solver backends (via good_lp):**
1. HiGHS (default, pure C, vendored) — fast LP/MIP solver, Apache-2.0
2. CBC (optional) — mature MIP solver from COIN-OR
3. CPLEX/Gurobi (optional, commercial) — for users who have licenses

## Implementation in FrankenMermaid
1. Add `good_lp` crate with HiGHS backend to fm-layout dependencies.
2. Implement `ConstraintLayoutSolver` that:
   a. Takes graph IR + Vec<LayoutConstraint> as input
   b. Creates LP variables for all node x,y coordinates
   c. Translates each LayoutConstraint into LP constraints
   d. For non-overlap: add MIP binary variables (only when constraint is present)
   e. Sets objective function (minimize total edge length, linearized)
   f. Solves with time limit
   g. Extracts node positions from solution
3. Implement warm-starting: when re-solving after incremental edit, use previous solution as initial point.
4. Implement infeasibility diagnosis: if constraints conflict, identify minimal infeasible subset (IIS).
5. Integrate with layout algorithm dispatch (bd-3uz.4): CP solver is selected when constraints are present.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] LP solver produces valid layouts for alignment + ordering constraints
- [ ] MIP solver handles non-overlap constraints for graphs up to 100 nodes
- [ ] Solve time < 1s for 200 nodes with LP constraints only
- [ ] Solve time < 5s for 100 nodes with MIP non-overlap constraints
- [ ] Time limit enforced; returns Sugiyama fallback on timeout
- [ ] Infeasibility diagnosis identifies conflicting constraints
- [ ] Warm-start reduces resolve time by >= 50% for incremental edits
- [ ] All constraint types from bd-1fef.1 supported

title: Benchmark constraint solver vs Sugiyama and publish adoption decision
description:
## Benchmark Constraint Solver vs Sugiyama (§9.7.3)

Comparative benchmark of constraint-based layout (LP/MIP) against Sugiyama baseline across diverse graph corpora and constraint scenarios, producing the adoption decision contract.

## Benchmark Design
**Dimensions:**
1. Graph size: {20, 50, 100, 200, 500} nodes
2. Graph density: {sparse (0.05), medium (0.15), dense (0.3)}
3. Constraint load: {none, light (2 alignment), medium (5 mixed), heavy (10+ mixed with non-overlap)}
4. Diagram type: {flowchart, class diagram, sequence backbone, state machine}

**Metrics per scenario:**
- Solve time (ms) — wall clock
- Layout quality score: weighted sum of edge length, crossing count, bounding box area, constraint satisfaction
- Memory usage (peak RSS delta)
- Constraint violation count (for Sugiyama baseline which ignores constraints)

**Comparison protocol:**
1. Run both solvers on identical input
2. Score both outputs on the same quality metric
3. For constraint scenarios: count constraint violations in Sugiyama output
4. Statistical analysis: paired t-test or Wilcoxon signed-rank across corpus

## Key Questions to Answer
- At what graph size does CP solver become impractical (> 5s solve time)?
- What constraint types benefit most from CP (alignment? non-overlap? grouping)?
- Is hybrid approach viable: Sugiyama for initial layout, CP for constraint repair?
- What is the quality improvement of CP over post-hoc constraint enforcement on Sugiyama output?

## Decision Contract Output
The benchmark produces a binding decision:
- **Full CP adoption:** CP solver is primary layout for constrained diagrams
- **Hybrid adoption:** Sugiyama primary, CP for constraint repair phase
- **Reject:** CP overhead not justified; implement constraints as Sugiyama post-processing
- **Deferred:** More work needed on solver performance; revisit after MIP warm-start optimization

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Benchmark covers all 4 dimensions (5*3*4*4 = 240 scenarios)
- [ ] Statistical analysis with confidence intervals (not just means)
- [ ] Quality metric is well-defined and documented
- [ ] Decision contract addresses all 4 key questions
- [ ] Results reproducible (deterministic inputs, fixed solver parameters)
- [ ] Criterion integration for CI regression detection

title: Cache-Oblivious Layout for Large Diagram Traversal
description:
## Cache-Oblivious Layout for Large Diagram Traversal

Apply cache-oblivious data structure principles to the graph layout pipeline, organizing node and edge data in memory to minimize cache misses during layout algorithms that traverse the graph structure.

## Mathematical Foundation
Cache-oblivious algorithms achieve optimal cache complexity without knowing the cache parameters (line size B, cache size M). The key technique is the van Emde Boas layout: store a tree/graph in memory so that any subtree of size <= M fits in O(M/B) cache lines.

**For graph layout:**
The Sugiyama algorithm traverses the graph in multiple passes: topological sort, rank assignment, ordering (per-layer), coordinate assignment. Each pass touches nodes in a different order. Cache-oblivious strategy:
1. **Space-filling curve ordering:** Store nodes in Z-order (Morton code) based on their 2D coordinates. Nodes that are spatially close are also close in memory → locality for force-directed and coordinate assignment passes.
2. **Cache-oblivious B-tree for adjacency:** Store adjacency lists in a vEB layout so that traversal of any connected subgraph has O(|subgraph| / B) cache misses.
3. **Blocked edge iteration:** Group edges by source rank for Sugiyama crossing minimization, ensuring per-layer iterations touch contiguous memory.

**Expected improvement:**
- Cache misses during layout: O(n / B) instead of O(n) (factor of B improvement, B typically 8-16 for 64-byte cache lines with 4-8 byte node IDs).
- For n = 10000 nodes: ~16x fewer L1 misses, ~4x fewer L2 misses (theoretical maximum).

## Key Papers
- Frigo, Leiserson, Prokop & Ramachandran, "Cache-Oblivious Algorithms" (FOCS 1999)
- Bender, Demaine & Farach-Colton, "Cache-Oblivious B-Trees" (SICOMP 2005)
- Arge, Goodrich, Nelson & Sitchinava, "Fundamental Parallel Algorithms for Private-Cache Chip Multiprocessors" (SPAA 2008) — cache-oblivious graph algorithms

## Implementation in FrankenMermaid
1. Implement Morton code (Z-order curve) computation for 2D coordinates.
2. After initial layout: reorder node storage array by Morton code.
3. Reorder adjacency list entries to match node storage order.
4. For incremental layout: maintain Z-order invariant on cache (re-sort on significant coordinate changes).
5. Benchmark: L1/L2 cache miss counts using perf counters (linux perf) before and after reordering.
6. Decision contract: adopt if cache misses reduced >= 30% AND layout time reduced >= 10%.

## Graveyard Reference: Cache-oblivious algorithms appear across graveyard in data structure contexts.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Morton code Z-order computation for 2D node positions
- [ ] Node array reordering by Z-order after layout
- [ ] Adjacency list reordering to match node order
- [ ] Cache miss reduction measured via perf counters (or cachegrind)
- [ ] Layout time improvement >= 10% on 5000+ node graphs
- [ ] No functional change to layout output (determinism preserved)
- [ ] Decision contract with specific adopt/reject thresholds
close_reason: Implemented cache-oblivious layout primitives in fm-layout/src/cache_oblivious.rs with: (1) Morton code Z-order curve encoding/decoding for 2D spatial locality (integer + float variants with bounding box mapping). (2) morton_order() permutation for reordering node arrays by spatial locality. (3) BlockedEdgeGroups for rank-grouped edge iteration (cache-friendly crossing minimization). (4) Van Emde Boas tree layout for recursive halving memory order. 17 tests: Morton code arithmetic, roundtrip, locality preservation, f64 range mapping, clamping, ordering determinism, cluster grouping, blocked edge groups, vEB permutation validity. All quality gates pass.

title: EPIC: Testing & Fault Injection for Alien Concepts
description:
## Testing & Fault Injection for Alien Concepts

Comprehensive fault injection testing framework that verifies FrankenMermaid's alien CS implementations degrade gracefully under adversarial conditions: memory pressure, CPU budget exhaustion, malformed inputs, platform-specific edge cases, and concurrent access patterns.

## Motivation
Alien CS concepts introduce complexity. Each has failure modes distinct from conventional code:
- E-graphs can explode in memory
- CGA rotors can denormalize under floating-point error accumulation
- Constraint solvers can hit infeasible configurations
- Bidirectional lenses can violate lens laws on edge-case inputs
- Incremental layout can have stale cache entries

Fault injection testing systematically exercises these failure modes to verify that FrankenMermaid handles them gracefully (structured error, fallback, degradation) rather than catastrophically (panic, hang, OOM, wrong output).

## Approach
1. **Environmental faults:** memory limits, CPU throttling, disk full, network loss (WASM)
2. **Input faults:** malformed Mermaid, adversarial graph structures, NaN/Infinity coordinates
3. **Algorithmic faults:** force E-graph budget exhaustion, force solver timeout, inject rotor denormalization
4. **Temporal faults:** race conditions in incremental layout cache, concurrent diagram edits
5. **Platform faults:** f64 precision differences across targets (x86 80-bit extended vs wasm 64-bit)

## Success Metrics
- Every alien concept has >= 3 dedicated fault injection tests
- Zero panics under any fault scenario (all faults produce structured errors or graceful degradation)
- Fault injection tests run in CI (< 5 minutes total)
- Coverage of all fallback paths verified (fallback code is exercised, not dead code)

title: E-graph memory explosion and budget exhaustion fault tests
description:
## E-Graph Memory Explosion Fault Tests

Test that E-graph-based crossing minimization (bd-1xma) handles memory and node budget exhaustion gracefully across all graph sizes and densities.

## Fault Scenarios
1. **Node budget hit:** Dense graph (K_{20,20} bipartite) forces e-graph to exceed max_enodes limit. Verify: fallback to greedy, structured diagnostic emitted, no OOM.
2. **Time budget hit:** Chain of 100 layers, each with 50 nodes. Force equality saturation to exceed wall-clock timeout. Verify: extraction of best-so-far, fallback comparison.
3. **Memory limit:** Set process memory limit (via setrlimit or cgroups) to 50MB, run e-graph on medium graph. Verify: graceful OOM handling, not process crash.
4. **Pathological rewrite loops:** Craft graph where rewrite rules produce many equivalent but non-convergent orderings. Verify: iteration limit kicks in.
5. **Zero-node layer:** Empty layer in Sugiyama should not crash e-graph (degenerate case).
6. **Single-node layer:** Layer with 1 node — e-graph is trivial, verify no overhead.

## Implementation
1. Use custom allocator wrapper to track and limit e-graph memory.
2. Use `std::time::Instant` with configurable timeout (not wall-clock dependent — use deterministic step counting for reproducibility).
3. Each fault test asserts: (a) no panic, (b) valid layout produced, (c) structured diagnostic emitted, (d) output is deterministic across 10 runs.
4. Parameterized tests: vary graph size and density to find the exact threshold where budget kicks in.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] All 6 fault scenarios tested
- [ ] Zero panics in any scenario
- [ ] Fallback produces valid layout within 100ms
- [ ] Structured diagnostic includes: budget_type, value, limit, strategy
- [ ] Output deterministic across 10 runs per scenario
- [ ] Tests run in < 30 seconds total

title: CGA rotor denormalization and floating-point edge case tests
description:
## CGA Rotor Denormalization and Floating-Point Edge Case Tests

Test that CGA rotor operations (bd-2q3f) remain numerically stable under long transform chains, extreme coordinates, and floating-point edge cases.

## Fault Scenarios
1. **Rotor denormalization after chained composition:** Compose 10000 small rotations (0.001 rad each). Verify rotor norm stays within [1-ε, 1+ε] or is explicitly renormalized. Without renormalization, norm drift can cause progressive scaling artifacts.
2. **Extreme coordinates:** Apply rotor to point at (1e15, 1e15). Verify: no Infinity, no NaN, result within expected range. CGA embedding squares coordinates, so (1e15)² = 1e30 is near f64 precision limit.
3. **Near-zero rotation:** Rotation by 1e-15 radians. Verify: cos(θ/2) ≈ 1, sin(θ/2) ≈ θ/2, rotor is valid (not degenerate).
4. **Near-π rotation:** Rotation by π - 1e-15 radians (almost 180°). Gimbal-lock-like scenario for rotors. Verify: correct transform, no sign flip errors.
5. **Zero translation:** Translation by (0, 0). Verify: identity rotor, no wasted computation.
6. **Negative scale:** Scale by -1 (reflection). Verify: correct reflection, rotor norm = 1.
7. **NaN input:** Apply rotor to point (NaN, 0). Verify: structured error, not silent propagation.
8. **Subnormal floats:** Coordinates near f64::MIN_POSITIVE. Verify: no flush-to-zero artifacts.

## Implementation
1. Each scenario is a parameterized test with exact expected outputs (computed analytically or via high-precision library like rug).
2. For scenario 1: compare accumulated rotor against direct construction of rotor for 10 radians, measure norm drift.
3. Use `#[should_panic]` for NaN input if design choice is to panic, or assert error return if design choice is Result.
4. Cross-platform: run on x86_64 (80-bit extended precision intermediate) and wasm32 (strict 64-bit) to detect precision divergence.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] All 8 fault scenarios tested
- [ ] Rotor norm drift < 1e-10 after 10000 compositions (with renormalization strategy documented)
- [ ] No NaN or Infinity in any scenario except NaN input (which produces structured error)
- [ ] Cross-platform determinism: same results on x86_64 and wasm32 (to within 1 ULP)
- [ ] Renormalization strategy documented and tested
- [ ] Tests run in < 10 seconds total

comments.author: PeachGorge
comments.text:
BLOCKED — br refuses the claim ('cannot claim blocked issue: bd-2q3f'), so I did not work it. Two things found while reading, both worth having before someone does.

SCENARIO 6 CONTRADICTS THE IMPLEMENTATION. This bead asks to 'Scale by -1 (reflection). Verify: correct reflection, rotor norm = 1.' Rotor::scale cannot do that — it asserts:

    assert!(factor > 0.0, "scale factor must be positive, got {factor}");

and is documented '# Panics if factor is not positive (ln of non-positive is undefined)', because it builds the rotor from ln(factor)/2. So scenario 6 as written tests a reflection API that does not exist. A dilation rotor in the conformal model is inherently positive-scale; a reflection is a different operation (an odd versor), not a negative dilation. Whoever picks this up must first DECIDE: assert the panic as the contract, or implement reflection separately. Writing a test that expects a reflection from scale(-1) would just fail, and 'fixing' it by relaxing the assert would let ln(-1) = NaN into every downstream rotor.

SCENARIO 1 IS THE ONE LIKELY TO BITE. It requires norm drift < 1e-10 after 10,000 compositions. Rotor::compose does NOT multiply in the even subalgebra — it round-trips through to_multivector, a full 16-component Multivector::geometric_product, and from_multivector. That is far more arithmetic per step than a rotor product needs, so drift over 10k steps is plausible and the bead's acceptance criterion may not hold as implemented. Related measured evidence on bd-9mqa: that same round-trip makes composition 10-40x slower than direct affine matrices.

PRIOR ART, so the next lane does not re-find these: the extreme-coordinate and NaN scenarios (2, 7, 8) are already partly covered by work landed this session on the same module — cga_queries_never_produce_non_finite_output_for_finite_input sweeps 20,000 configurations at f64::MAX / 1e300 / 1e150 / MIN_POSITIVE / signed zero and asserts no panic, no non-finite coordinate, no NaN distance. That sweep found three real defects under 395 previously-green tests (inf*0.0 NaN surviving clamp; NaN distance for finite points; the conformal d^2 identity resolving 1e-9 as exactly 0.0). Scenarios 2/7/8 should extend that sweep rather than start a parallel one.

ALSO NOTE the acceptance criterion 'same results on x86_64 and wasm32 to within 1 ULP' needs a wasm32 runner; nothing in the current gate setup executes wasm tests, so that criterion cannot be met by cargo test alone.

title: Constraint solver infeasibility and timeout fault tests
description:
## Constraint Solver Infeasibility and Timeout Fault Tests

Test that the constraint programming layout solver (bd-1fef) handles infeasible constraints, solver timeouts, and degenerate inputs gracefully.

## Fault Scenarios
1. **Contradictory constraints:** "A left_of B" AND "B left_of A". Verify: infeasibility detected, minimal conflicting set identified, Sugiyama fallback used.
2. **Over-constrained layout:** 50 alignment constraints on a 20-node graph with conflicting geometry. Verify: solver reports infeasibility, identifies which constraints conflict.
3. **Solver timeout:** 1000-node graph with 100 non-overlap constraints (requires MIP). Set timeout to 100ms. Verify: timeout handler returns best feasible solution found so far (or Sugiyama fallback).
4. **Unbounded problem:** Constraints that allow coordinates to grow without bound (missing bounding constraint). Verify: solver detects unbounded solution, adds implicit bounds.
5. **Empty graph:** Zero nodes, zero constraints. Verify: empty layout returned, no solver invocation.
6. **Single node:** One node, one pin constraint. Verify: trivial solution, no solver overhead.
7. **Constraint on non-existent node:** Alignment constraint references node ID not in graph. Verify: validation error before solver invocation.
8. **Numerical instability:** Constraints with very large coefficients (1e15) or very small (1e-15). Verify: solver handles without numerical breakdown.

## Implementation
1. Use the constraint DSL from bd-1fef.1 to construct test scenarios.
2. Mock solver time limit to force timeouts deterministically.
3. For infeasibility tests: verify IIS (Irreducible Infeasible Subset) is minimal.
4. For timeout tests: verify partial solution is feasible (all hard constraints satisfied).
5. Each test asserts: no panic, valid output (even if degraded), structured diagnostic.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] All 8 fault scenarios tested
- [ ] Infeasibility detection with minimal conflicting set for scenarios 1-2
- [ ] Timeout produces valid partial solution or Sugiyama fallback
- [ ] Validation catches non-existent node references before solver
- [ ] Zero panics, zero OOM across all scenarios
- [ ] Structured diagnostics emitted for all fault conditions
- [ ] Tests run in < 20 seconds total

title: Incremental layout cache staleness and consistency fault tests
description:
## Incremental Layout Cache Staleness and Consistency Fault Tests

Test that incremental subgraph re-layout (bd-20fq) handles cache staleness, dependency graph corruption, and concurrent edit patterns without producing incorrect layouts.

## Fault Scenarios
1. **Stale cache entry:** Manually corrupt a cached subgraph layout (flip x/y coordinates). Verify: validation detects stale entry, triggers re-computation, emits diagnostic.
2. **Dependency graph cycle:** Inject a circular dependency (subgraph A depends on B, B depends on A). Verify: cycle detected, full re-layout triggered as fallback.
3. **Missing dependency:** Remove a dependency edge from the tracking graph. Verify: dirty propagation still works (may miss some invalidations, caught by checksum verification).
4. **Rapid sequential edits:** 100 edits in 10ms (faster than layout can process). Verify: coalescing works, final layout is correct, intermediate states don't leak.
5. **Concurrent edits to same subgraph:** Two edit operations targeting the same subgraph simultaneously. Verify: serialization or last-writer-wins, no data corruption.
6. **Edit during layout computation:** Start a layout computation, then inject an edit before it completes. Verify: layout restarts or queues the edit, doesn't produce mixed old/new results.
7. **Cache overflow:** Fill cache with 10000 subgraph entries, trigger eviction. Verify: eviction policy is LRU/LFU, re-computation on miss is correct.
8. **Cross-subgraph edge edit:** Add an edge that connects two previously independent subgraphs. Verify: both subgraphs invalidated and re-laid-out together.

## Implementation
1. Use internal testing hooks to inject cache corruption and dependency graph mutations.
2. For concurrent tests: use `std::thread::scope` or `tokio::test` with controlled scheduling.
3. For rapid edit tests: programmatic edit API, not user input simulation.
4. Each test verifies: final layout == full-recompute layout (bit-identical check).
5. Measure cache hit rate and re-computation count per scenario.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] All 8 fault scenarios tested
- [ ] Final layout always matches full-recompute (the golden invariant)
- [ ] Cycle detection works and emits structured diagnostic
- [ ] Rapid edit coalescing produces correct final result
- [ ] No data races (run under Miri or ThreadSanitizer)
- [ ] Cache eviction does not cause incorrect layouts
- [ ] Tests run in < 15 seconds total
close_reason: Completed: 6 fault tests added — stale cache structural validity, rapid 100-edit coalescing, cross-subgraph edge invalidation, direction-change cache key mismatch, edit-undo stability (10 rounds), node size cache consistency. Known finding documented: derive_layout_edits doesn't detect pure edge-topology changes (same node count). 348 fm-layout tests pass, all quality gates clean.

title: Bidirectional lens law violation detection and recovery tests
description:
## Bidirectional Lens Law Violation Detection and Recovery Tests

Test that bidirectional lenses (bd-1t7l) detect and recover from lens law violations caused by edge-case inputs, format ambiguities, and lossy transformations.

## Fault Scenarios
1. **Ambiguous parse round-trip:** Mermaid source that parses to the same AST from multiple text representations (e.g., `A --> B` vs `A-->B`). Verify: GetPut returns ONE canonical form, not the original (acceptable deviation documented).
2. **Comment preservation failure:** Source with comments between nodes. After diagram edit (put), verify comments are preserved in correct positions (not dropped, not moved to wrong location).
3. **Directive loss:** Source with `%%{init: ...}%%` directives. After round-trip, verify directives preserved verbatim.
4. **Multi-line node label:** Node with multi-line label containing special characters (`"Line1\nLine2"`). Verify: round-trip preserves label exactly.
5. **Layout-dependent source ordering:** Diagram where visual left-to-right ordering differs from source text ordering. After drag-to-reorder in diagram, verify source text updated correctly.
6. **Lossy layout information:** Diagram rendered with force-directed layout (continuous coordinates). After put, verify source text does not contain coordinate artifacts.
7. **Empty diagram round-trip:** Empty mermaid source → empty diagram → empty source. Verify: identity.
8. **Maximum complexity:** 500-node diagram with subgraphs, styling, click events, links. Full round-trip. Verify: no information loss.

## Implementation
1. For each scenario: compute get(s), then put(s, get(s)), then compare with s (GetPut law).
2. For put direction: modify the view (move node, add edge), compute put(s, v'), then get(put(s, v')), compare with v' (PutGet law).
3. Use exact string comparison for source text (after whitespace normalization).
4. For lossy cases: document the acceptable deviation and test that deviation is within bounds.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] All 8 fault scenarios tested
- [ ] GetPut law verified for all scenarios (with documented acceptable deviations)
- [ ] PutGet law verified for node move, add, delete operations
- [ ] Comment and directive preservation verified
- [ ] Multi-line labels round-trip correctly
- [ ] No information loss on complex diagrams
- [ ] Acceptable deviations documented in evidence ledger

title: Cross-platform floating-point determinism fault tests
description:
## Cross-Platform Floating-Point Determinism Fault Tests

Test that layout output is bit-identical across x86_64, aarch64, and wasm32 targets, detecting platform-specific floating-point behavior that could break determinism guarantees.

## Fault Scenarios
1. **x87 80-bit intermediate precision:** On x86_64, some floating-point operations may use 80-bit extended precision registers, producing different results from the same operations on aarch64 (64-bit only) or wasm32 (strict 64-bit). Verify: all layout coordinates identical across platforms.
2. **FMA (fused multiply-add) difference:** aarch64 has hardware FMA which computes a*b+c with single rounding. x86_64 may or may not use FMA. Verify: FMA difference does not affect layout output (or FMA is explicitly controlled).
3. **Subnormal handling:** Some ARM configurations flush subnormals to zero. Verify: no subnormal results in layout coordinates (or explicit flush-to-zero everywhere).
4. **Math library differences:** sin(), cos(), sqrt() implementations may differ by 1 ULP across platforms. Verify: CGA rotor operations that use trig functions produce identical results (or use a portable math library).
5. **NaN propagation:** IEEE 754 allows different NaN payloads and quiet/signaling behavior across platforms. Verify: no NaN in layout output on any platform.
6. **Rounding mode:** Different default rounding modes (round-to-nearest-even vs round-to-nearest-away). Verify: layout uses explicit rounding mode or results are rounding-mode-independent.

## Implementation
1. Create a "golden output" test that computes layout for a diverse corpus and stores SHA-256 of coordinates.
2. Run the same test on all three targets: x86_64 (native), aarch64 (cross-compile + QEMU or native), wasm32 (wasmtime).
3. Compare SHA-256 hashes across targets.
4. If mismatches found: bisect to the specific operation and coordinate that differs.
5. Fix strategies: (a) use `#[cfg(target_arch)]` to force consistent behavior, (b) use portable math library (libm crate), (c) avoid trig in hot paths.
6. For CGA operations: consider using integer arithmetic or fixed-point for the determinism-critical path.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Layout SHA-256 identical across x86_64, aarch64, wasm32 for entire test corpus
- [ ] Trig function portability verified (libm crate or equivalent)
- [ ] Subnormal handling documented and consistent
- [ ] FMA impact assessed and mitigated if needed
- [ ] No NaN in any layout output on any platform
- [ ] Test runs in CI for all three targets

title: Swiss Table hash collision and DoS resistance tests
description:
## Swiss Table Hash Collision and DoS Resistance Tests

Test that FxHash-based Swiss Tables (bd-2gr9) are resistant to crafted hash collisions and degenerate performance patterns, verifying the security analysis that non-cryptographic hashing is safe for internally-generated IDs.

## Fault Scenarios
1. **Crafted FxHash collisions:** Generate a set of NodeId values that all hash to the same bucket under FxHash. Verify: performance degrades linearly (O(n) probe chain), not catastrophically, and stays within acceptable bounds.
2. **Worst-case load factor:** Fill a NodeMap to 99% capacity (beyond the 87.5% resize threshold). Verify: resize triggers correctly, no probe chain exceeds O(log n).
3. **Sequential ID pathology:** Test that sequential NodeId(0), NodeId(1), ..., NodeId(10000) do NOT create clustering under FxHash. Measure probe chain distribution.
4. **Mixed insert/delete pattern:** Alternate insert and delete operations to create tombstone accumulation. Verify: Swiss Table handles tombstones correctly (rehash on high tombstone density).
5. **Memory allocation failure during resize:** Mock allocator to fail during HashMap resize. Verify: no data loss, operation returns error, existing data remains accessible.
6. **Concurrent read during resize:** (If lock-free or concurrent map is used) Read access during resize operation. Verify: consistent snapshot semantics.

## Implementation
1. For collision crafting: reverse-engineer FxHash for specific inputs (FxHash is simple multiply-shift, collisions are constructible).
2. Benchmark probe chain length distribution for each scenario.
3. Compare performance under worst case vs SipHash (the cryptographic alternative) to quantify the security/performance tradeoff.
4. Document the threat model: who controls NodeId values? (Answer: parser only, not user input. Therefore HashDoS is not a realistic threat.)

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Crafted collisions cause graceful degradation, not crash or hang
- [ ] Probe chain distribution for sequential IDs is uniform (no clustering)
- [ ] Tombstone accumulation handled by automatic rehash
- [ ] Threat model documented: internal IDs = no HashDoS risk
- [ ] Performance comparison with SipHash for the worst-case scenario
- [ ] All tests deterministic and run in < 10 seconds

title: End-to-end alien concept integration fault test suite
description:
## End-to-End Alien Concept Integration Fault Test Suite

Integration tests that exercise multiple alien concepts simultaneously under fault conditions, verifying that interactions between E-graphs, CGA, constraint solver, incremental layout, and bidirectional lenses do not produce emergent failures.

## Fault Scenarios (Multi-Concept Interactions)
1. **E-graph fallback + constraint solver:** E-graph exceeds budget, falls back to Sugiyama, then constraint solver applies constraints to the Sugiyama result. Verify: constraints still satisfied, layout valid.
2. **CGA transform + incremental re-layout:** Edit a node, incremental re-layout computes new coordinates for dirty subgraph using CGA rotor composition. Verify: CGA and non-CGA subgraphs stitch together correctly.
3. **Bidirectional lens + constraint solver:** User drags a constrained node in the diagram. Lens put must update source text while respecting constraint semantics. Verify: PutGet law holds, constraints in source text updated.
4. **Swiss Table + E-graph:** E-graph stores equivalent orderings in FxHash-backed maps. Under budget pressure, extraction accesses many map entries. Verify: no hash collision performance issue in extraction.
5. **All concepts simultaneously:** 200-node diagram with constraints, processed with E-graph crossing minimization, rendered via CGA transform pipeline, with incremental re-layout enabled. Edit one node, verify full pipeline produces correct result within 500ms.
6. **Cascading fallback:** E-graph fails → greedy Sugiyama → constraint solver times out → unconstrained Sugiyama. Three levels of fallback. Verify: each degradation produces valid output and diagnostic.
7. **Memory pressure on full pipeline:** Set 200MB process memory limit. Run full pipeline on 500-node diagram. Verify: all concepts degrade gracefully within memory budget.

## Implementation
1. Each scenario is an integration test that constructs a specific diagram, configures the pipeline, and injects specific faults.
2. Use environment variables or test fixtures to control budget/timeout settings.
3. Verify final output against golden checksums (from bd-17e4.2).
4. Measure total pipeline latency and memory for each scenario.
5. Test both native (x86_64) and WASM targets.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] All 7 multi-concept interaction scenarios tested
- [ ] Zero panics, zero data corruption across all scenarios
- [ ] Cascading fallback chain works end-to-end
- [ ] Memory-constrained pipeline stays within budget
- [ ] Golden checksum verification passes for non-degraded outputs
- [ ] All diagnostic events structured and machine-parseable
- [ ] Tests run in < 60 seconds total
